expectBivy: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout

bivy.name: Meadows below the Silver Horn's south face
bivy.notes: The camp for both routes on the south face, in the meadows at about 6,200 ft where the creek draining the Silver Horn's south side opens out below the white granite. Reached from the Cedar Creek Trailhead: about five miles up the Cedar Creek Trail, then right below the old burn onto a rough path up the right-hand side of that creek. This is not the Wine Spires pullout or Burgundy Col — those serve the other side of the crest and do not reach this face. It is a rarely visited corner with no established climbers' camp and little traffic, so expect to pick your own spot on the meadow.
bivy.water: The creek the approach path follows is the water source on the way up. How late in the season it still runs at the meadows is not recorded, so carry enough capacity for a dry camp late in a dry year.
bivy.permit: No reservation, no quota and no overnight permit; national forest dispersed-camping rules apply. A Northwest Forest Pass, an Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking at the Cedar Creek Trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Open meadow with room for a few tents; no established sites

Road: USFS Cedar Creek Trailhead page (FR 5310-200, south side of SR-20 between MP 175-176, ~0.5 mi E of Klipchuck turnoff, gravel-pit parking, 3,030 ft, vault toilet, no water) + WTA Cedar Falls (FR 200, 0.8 mi to trailhead) + WTA Cedar Falls Snowshoe (SR-20 closed at MP 178 Jan-Mar, may be plowed to MP 171 gate Dec/Apr, can stop without warning). road.name: SR-20 and FR 5310-200 to the Cedar Creek Trailhead
road.status: Short forest spur of about 0.8 mile from SR-20 to the parking area by a gravel pit at the road's end (about 3,030 ft). Vault toilet, no potable water.
road.driveNote: From Winthrop, drive about 18 miles west on SR-20 and turn south onto FR 5310-200 between mileposts 175 and 176, about half a mile east of the Klipchuck Campground turnoff. Follow it to its end; the trail starts at the southeast end of the gravel pit.
road.seasonalGate: The trailhead is east of the Washington Pass winter closure, so it does not wait for the pass to open, but FR 5310-200 is not plowed. From January to March SR-20 is usually closed at milepost 178, about 2.5 miles short of the turnoff; in December and April it may be plowed to the gate at milepost 171, and that plowing can stop without warning until the spring clearing.

bivy.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. Parties climbing the South Buttress or Southeast Buttress routinely sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
bivy.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
bivy.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to the Cutthroat Creek trailhead, a short drive east on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
bivy.water: Potable water provided in season, shut off once the campground closes for the year.
bivy.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: 27 sites, tents and small RVs

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
bivy.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
bivy.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
bivy.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

bivy.name: Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy, south side
bivy.notes: Serves every route reached through the basin south of the peak: the South and Complete South Buttress, the Southeast Buttress, the East Face lines over the rib, and the North Ridge by its usual approach, which bears right out of the same basin toward the North Ridge Notch. The way in starts from the long pullout on the north side of SR 20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, not from the Cutthroat Lake trail on the east side of the pass: a cairned track leaves the pullout's east end, drops through timber to cross State Creek, and climbs meadows into the bowl, roughly two hours with a pack. Parties camp here to take a long route in a single push rather than commit to a headlamp descent. Ground is a mix of heather bench and talus and the pads are small, so a large party will be split up. The meadows are thin and the basin sees enough traffic to show it.
bivy.water: A stream runs through the basin and is generally reliable through the climbing season, fed by snow patches under the peak. Late-season flow can thin, so carry capacity for a dry night in a hot September.
bivy.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit, no reservation and no quota — the opposite of the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Several scattered one- and two-tent pads in the meadows and among the boulders; no established camp, so parties spread out

wa_complete_south_buttress.why: TASK 2 (south-side bivy): old note said the path leaves the Cutthroat Lake trail and that the bivy does not serve the North Ridge. Every carrying route's own approach starts at the SR-20 pullout ~1.5 mi W of Washington Pass and crosses State Creek (Mountain Project South Buttress; trailcatjim State Creek report; Mountaineers SE Buttress summary); the Cutthroat Lake trail starts at the Cutthroat Creek TH near MP 167, east of the pass (WTA). North Ridge standard approach is 'as for the South Buttress, veering right ... to gain the basin SE of Cutthroat Peak' (Mountain Project North Ridge) — so the basin bivy does serve it. Renamed to drop 'SOUTH-SIDE routes only'; water/permit/capacity untouched.

Renamed to drop 'SOUTH-SIDE routes only'; water/permit/capacity untouched.

bivy.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. Parties climbing the South Buttress or Southeast Buttress routinely sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
bivy.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
bivy.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to the Cutthroat Creek trailhead, a short drive east on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
bivy.water: Potable water provided in season, shut off once the campground closes for the year.
bivy.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: 27 sites, tents and small RVs

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
bivy.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
bivy.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
bivy.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

bivy.name: Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy, south side
bivy.notes: Serves every route reached through the basin south of the peak: the South and Complete South Buttress, the Southeast Buttress, the East Face lines over the rib, and the North Ridge by its usual approach, which bears right out of the same basin toward the North Ridge Notch. The way in starts from the long pullout on the north side of SR 20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, not from the Cutthroat Lake trail on the east side of the pass: a cairned track leaves the pullout's east end, drops through timber to cross State Creek, and climbs meadows into the bowl, roughly two hours with a pack. Parties camp here to take a long route in a single push rather than commit to a headlamp descent. Ground is a mix of heather bench and talus and the pads are small, so a large party will be split up. The meadows are thin and the basin sees enough traffic to show it.
bivy.water: A stream runs through the basin and is generally reliable through the climbing season, fed by snow patches under the peak. Late-season flow can thin, so carry capacity for a dry night in a hot September.
bivy.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit, no reservation and no quota — the opposite of the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Several scattered one- and two-tent pads in the meadows and among the boulders; no established camp, so parties spread out

bivy.name: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure
bivy.notes: The lake sits about 1.8 miles in with roughly 500 ft of gain, in the basin under the peak's north and east sides. It is a pleasant place to stage, but the quarter-mile closure exists because the shoreline was being loved to death and it is enforced rather than advisory. It does not serve Cutthroat Peak's south-side routes or the usual North Ridge approach: those start from a different trailhead, a long pullout on SR 20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, and cross State Creek into the basin south of the peak, so for them treat this as a rest-day or bad-weather option rather than a staging camp.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet stream are dependable all season. Treat or filter.
bivy.permit: No permit needed, but a hard rule applies: NO overnight camping within a quarter mile of Cutthroat Lake. Camp outside that radius and you are legal with no paperwork.
bivy.capacity: Limited and regulated — the usable ground is set back from the water, so realistically a handful of small parties

It does not: south-side routes start at the SR-20 pullout ~1.5 mi W of Washington Pass and cross State Creek (Mountain Project South Buttress + North Ridge; trailcatjim); Cutthroat Lake trail starts at Cutthroat Creek road 400 near MP 167 (WTA). Only the one sentence changed. The camp does fit this Molar Tooth route (its approach 1 passes Cutthroat Lake).

bivy.name: Hogsback Camp, Heliotrope Ridge
bivy.notes: The default first night for parties on the Coleman-Deming and the usual staging point for the North Ridge, on the moraine bench above the trail's stream crossings about 2.5 to 3 miles in. Glacier Creek Road, the only driving approach, washed out in the December 2025 floods; the repairs were finished and vehicles could again reach the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead from 20 August 2026. The road has washed out before, so check its status before an early- or late-season trip. Waste handling has varied year to year, with toilets present some seasons and pack-it-out blue bags the rule in others, so carry bags regardless. Snow usually covers the camp until well into June, which makes a flat platform easier to find and liquid water harder.
bivy.water: Melt streams run below the moraine and near the trail crossings through most of the climbing season, but they retreat with the snowpack and can be gone or badly silted by late August — carry a stove capable of melting snow late in the year
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit; camping is dispersed and unregulated apart from wilderness rules (12-person party limit, no campfires at this elevation). A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Numerous flat gravel and snow platforms along the moraine crest; the busiest camp on the north side and it fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: North Ridge glacier bivy, upper Coleman
bivy.notes: North Ridge parties generally carry from the Hogsback out onto the Coleman and bivy somewhere around 6,800 to 7,000 ft to shorten the approach to the base of the ridge, which itself rises around 4,000 ft to the summit. Where exactly that camp sits is decided by crevasse conditions on the day rather than by any fixed location, so it is worth arriving with daylight left to scout. The camp is on glacier, exposed, and above the point where you can retreat without roping up. Road access is the same as for the Hogsback: Glacier Creek Road reopened to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead on 20 August 2026 after the flood repairs.
bivy.water: None reliable. Melt snow, and carry enough fuel for a party that will also be melting for the climb.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit required to camp. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Dug snow platforms for one or two parties; no established site, and the usable spot moves year to year

bivy.name: Kulshan Cabin site and Harrison Camp
bivy.notes: The cabin itself is long gone, and the name now marks a cluster of sites around 4,800 to 5,000 ft with Harrison Camp on the moraine above the lower Coleman. These suit a party arriving late, anyone who wants trees around them in bad weather, or a group that would rather climb from lower down than share the Hogsback. The trade-off is an extra thousand feet on summit day. Backcountry toilets have been maintained here in some seasons but not others, so plan to pack waste out.
bivy.water: Reliable — the approach streams below the moraine still carry water here later in the season than they do higher up, though the crossings themselves can run high and pushy on warm afternoons
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Heliotrope Ridge.
bivy.capacity: Several small forested and moraine-edge sites; more sheltered and lower-capacity than the Hogsback

bivy.name: Upper Coleman Glacier snow camps, below the Black Buttes
bivy.notes: Pushing camp onto the glacier below the Black Buttes cuts a real chunk out of summit day and puts you above most of the weather that sits on the moraine. It costs you a fully exposed camp on snow, so platforms need walls, and everything about the site depends on that year's crevasse pattern — what was a flat bench one August can be broken up the next. Parties are already roped and on glacier travel terrain to reach it, which rules it out for anyone wanting a simple carry. Wind is the usual reason people retreat from here to the Hogsback.
bivy.water: None you can rely on — this is a melt-snow camp, so budget fuel accordingly. Occasional surface runoff appears on the rock of the Black Buttes in hot spells but should not be planned around.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit for camping. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Whatever platforms your party digs; commonly used between roughly 7,000 and 7,200 ft, with room for a handful of tents but no established sites

bivy.name: Colfax-Grant saddle bivy
bivy.notes: The saddle between Colfax Peak and the main summit is occasionally used as a very high bivy by strong parties shortening summit day, and more often as an emergency stop by parties caught out by weather or a slow descent. It is fully exposed to wind and to whatever the mountain is doing, with no shelter of any kind, and the Roman Wall above it is not somewhere to be improvising in a storm. Treat it as a contingency rather than a plan unless the forecast is settled and your party is fast. It is also the last place on the route with any option other than continuing up or going down.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, or carry everything from lower on the route.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit required. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties at most; an exposed high point rather than a campsite

bivy.name: Heliotrope Ridge Camp

expectBivy: Hogsback Camp
Coleman Glacier bivy under the Black Buttes north faces

bivy.name: Hogsback Camp
Coleman Glacier bivy under the Black Buttes north faces
bivy.notes: Colfax's three north-side ice lines — the Cosley-Houston, the Polish Route and Kimchi Suicide Volcano — all start off the Coleman somewhere near 8,000 ft, and this is the staging ground for a party that does not want to cover the whole approach from the Hogsback on climb morning. The important thing about it is where you do not put the tent: ice and rock come off the Colfax seracs onto this part of the glacier with some regularity, so the usable camping is out on the flats well clear of the fall line, never tucked in against the toe of the face because it looks sheltered. Many parties skip this camp entirely and climb these routes in a long day from the trailhead or from the Hogsback, which is a reasonable answer to the same hazard. These are cold-season routes, roughly late October into May, and the ice changes character completely across that window. Glacier Creek Road washed out in the December 2025 floods and reopened to vehicles all the way to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead on 20 August 2026. For a cold-season attempt, check how far up it can be driven before planning to carry a heavy load.
bivy.water: None to rely on. Melt snow. Surface runoff sometimes appears on the rock of the buttes in a hot spell and should not be planned around.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight permit; camping is dispersed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Heliotrope Ridge. Party limit 12, no campfires, no toilets on the route, waste packed out in blue bags available free from the ranger offices. Registering a climb is voluntary and worth doing.
bivy.capacity: Dug platforms for a party or two on the flats out from the foot of the faces; no established site and nothing to shelter behind
